claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a naturally formed native oxide film before exposure.
The native oxide film governs the corrosion behavior of untreated Q235 steel.
At room temperature, the native oxide film provides effective corrosion protection to Q235 steel.
During salt exposure at 700–900 °C, the native oxide film becomes compromised.
High-temperature thermal stresses induce phase transformations in the oxide film.
Salt-driven reactions at high temperature increase oxide-film porosity.
High-temperature exposure may cause oxide-film spallation.
Oxide-film phase transformation, porosity, or spallation exposes fresh metal.
Exposure of fresh metal accelerates corrosion of Q235 steel.
The continuity of the native iron oxide film mediates corrosion protection.
The phase composition of the native iron oxide film mediates corrosion protection.
The adhesion of the native iron oxide film mediates corrosion protection.
Relative to room-temperature salt exposure, high-temperature salt exposure will produce significantly greater mass change.
Relative to room-temperature salt exposure, high-temperature salt exposure will cause greater oxide-film degradation, evidenced by increased porosity, phase shifts, or spallation.
Relative to room-temperature salt exposure, high-temperature salt exposure will reduce surface mechanical integrity.
Untreated Q235 steel under room-temperature salt exposure maintains a relatively intact oxide film.
Untreated Q235 steel under room-temperature salt exposure has a low corrosion rate.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when annealing, engineered coatings, or other pretreatments have altered the oxide film.
The quantitative relationship between oxide-film transformation and corrosion rate may depend on exposure duration.
The quantitative relationship between oxide-film transformation and corrosion rate may depend on salt composition.
